claim: A screen yielded a sterile mutant, 'ketu', caused by a Ythdc2 missense mutation.
source: A screen yielded a sterile mutant, 'ketu', caused by a Ythdc2 missense mutation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing the identification and characterization of the ketu mutation.

claim: Mutant germ cells enter meiosis but proceed prematurely to aberrant metaphase and apoptosis.
source: Mutant germ cells enter meiosis but proceed prematurely to aberrant metaphase and apoptosis, and display defects in transitioning from spermatogonial to meiotic gene expression programs.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by histological and immunofluorescence data showing aberrant metaphase-like cells and increased apoptosis in mutant testes.

claim: ketu phenocopies mutants lacking MEIOC, a YTHDC2 partner.
source: ketu phenocopies mutants lacking MEIOC, a YTHDC2 partner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of phenotypes between ketu and Meioc mutants described in the manuscript and cited literature (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).

claim: YTHDC2 is cytoplasmic.
source: Consistent with roles in post-transcriptional regulation, YTHDC2 is cytoplasmic, has 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity in vitro, and has similarity within its YTH domain to an N6-methyladenosine recognition pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence data showing cytoplasmic localization of YTHDC2 in spermatocytes (Figure 7).

claim: YTHDC2 has 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity in vitro.
source: Consistent with roles in post-transcriptional regulation, YTHDC2 is cytoplasmic, has 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity in vitro, and has similarity within its YTH domain to an N6-methyladenosine recognition pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical assays showing ATP-dependent RNA unwinding activity on substrates with 3' single-stranded extensions (Figure 9).

claim: YTHDC2 has similarity within its YTH domain to an N6-methyladenosine recognition pocket.
source: Consistent with roles in post-transcriptional regulation, YTHDC2 is cytoplasmic, has 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity in vitro, and has similarity within its YTH domain to an N6-methyladenosine recognition pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis showing conservation of m6A-binding residues in the YTH domain (Figure 8).

claim: YTHDC2 orthologs are present throughout metazoans.
source: Orthologs are present throughout metazoans, but are diverged in nematodes and, more dramatically, Drosophilidae, where Bgcn is descended from a Ythdc2 gene duplication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing YTHDC2 homologs across metazoan species (Figure 10).

claim: YTHDC2 orthologs are diverged in nematodes.
source: Orthologs are present throughout metazoans, but are diverged in nematodes and, more dramatically, Drosophilidae, where Bgcn is descended from a Ythdc2 gene duplication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing structural divergence of nematode YTHDC2 homologs (Figure 10).

claim: Bgcn is descended from a Ythdc2 gene duplication in Drosophilidae.
source: Orthologs are present throughout metazoans, but are diverged in nematodes and, more dramatically, Drosophilidae, where Bgcn is descended from a Ythdc2 gene duplication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing Bgcn as a paralog of YTHDC2 in schizophoran flies (Figure 10).

claim: There is similarity between MEIOC and Bam, a Bgcn partner unique to schizophoran flies.
source: We also uncover similarity between MEIOC and Bam, a Bgcn partner unique to schizophoran flies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence alignment analysis showing remote similarity between MEIOC and Bam (Figure 11).

claim: Regulation of gene expression by YTHDC2-MEIOC is an evolutionarily ancient strategy for controlling the germline transition into meiosis.
source: We propose that regulation of gene expression by YTHDC2-MEIOC is an evolutionarily ancient strategy for controlling the germline transition into meiosis.
evidence: This is a proposal stated in the abstract based on the conservation of YTHDC2 and MEIOC across metazoans and their functional roles in meiotic entry.

claim: Meiosis achieves genome reduction by appending two rounds of chromosome segregation to one round of DNA replication.
source: The specialized cell division of meiosis achieves this genome reduction by appending two rounds of chromosome segregation to one round of DNA replication (Page and Hawley, 2003).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about meiosis supported by citation to Page and Hawley, 2003.

claim: Homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes segregate in the first meiotic division.
source: Homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes segregate in the first meiotic division, then sister centromeres separate in the second.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about meiosis supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Sister centromeres separate in the second meiotic division.
source: Homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes segregate in the first meiotic division, then sister centromeres separate in the second.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about meiosis supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Prior to the first division, homologous chromosomes pair and recombine to form temporary connections that stabilize the chromosomes on the metaphase I spindle.
source: Prior to the first division, homologous chromosomes pair and recombine to form temporary connections that stabilize the chromosomes on the metaphase I spindle (Page and Hawley, 2003; Hunter, 2007).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about meiosis supported by citations to Page and Hawley, 2003 and Hunter, 2007.

claim: Errors in meiotic processes can cause gametogenic failure and infertility.
source: Errors in these processes can cause gametogenic failure and infertility, or yield aneuploid gametes that in turn lead to miscarriage or birth defects in offspring (Hassold and Hunt, 2001; Sasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Hassold and Hunt, 2001 and Sasaki et al., 2010.

claim: Errors in meiotic processes can yield aneuploid gametes that lead to miscarriage or birth defects in offspring.
source: Errors in these processes can cause gametogenic failure and infertility, or yield aneuploid gametes that in turn lead to miscarriage or birth defects in offspring (Hassold and Hunt, 2001; Sasaki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Hassold and Hunt, 2001 and Sasaki et al., 2010.

claim: In well-studied metazoan species, meiosis occurs specifically in a dedicated germ cell lineage after a period of limited expansion via mitotic 'transit-amplifying' cell divisions.
source: In well-studied metazoan species, meiosis occurs specifically in a dedicated germ cell lineage after a period of limited expansion via mitotic 'transit-amplifying' cell divisions (de Rooij, 2001; Davies and Fuller, 2008).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to de Rooij, 2001 and Davies and Fuller, 2008.

claim: The coordination of germline stem cell divisions with entry into meiosis and the subsequent progression of cells through meiotic divisions are tightly regulated.
source: The coordination of germline stem cell divisions with entry into meiosis and the subsequent progression of cells through meiotic divisions are tightly regulated (e.g., Griswold, 2016), but mechanisms underlying this regulation are not fully understood, particularly in mammals.
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Griswold, 2016.

claim: Mechanisms underlying the regulation of germline stem cell divisions and meiotic progression are not fully understood, particularly in mammals.
source: The coordination of germline stem cell divisions with entry into meiosis and the subsequent progression of cells through meiotic divisions are tightly regulated (e.g., Griswold, 2016), but mechanisms underlying this regulation are not fully understood, particularly in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge, supported by citation to Griswold, 2016.

claim: The catalog of mammalian genes required for germ cell development, meiosis, and gametogenesis remains incomplete.
source: And, more generally, the catalog of mammalian genes required for germ cell development, meiosis, and gametogenesis remains incomplete.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge based on general understanding of the field.

claim: A phenotype-based, random chemical mutagenesis screen was carried out to identify novel mouse meiotic mutants.
source: In efforts to overcome this lack, we carried out a phenotype-based, random chemical mutagenesis screen to identify novel mouse meiotic mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the description of the screen methodology in the Results section.

claim: One hit from the screen was a male-sterile mutant named rahu.
source: One hit was a male-sterile mutant we named rahu, for 'recombination-affected with hypogonadism from under-populated testes' (Jain et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation to Jain et al., 2017.

claim: The rahu mutant is defective for the function of a rodent-specific DNA methyltransferase paralog, DNMT3C.
source: This mutant is defective for the function of a rodent-specific DNA methyltransferase paralog, DNMT3C.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation to Jain et al., 2017.

claim: ketu is a missense mutation in Ythdc2.
source: ketu is a missense mutation in Ythdc2 (YTH-domain containing 2), which encodes a protein with RNA helicase motifs and a YT521-B homology (YTH) RNA-binding domain (Stoilov et al., 2002; Morohashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by experimental data showing the identification of the mutation (Figure 2).

claim: Ythdc2 encodes a protein with RNA helicase motifs and a YT521-B homology (YTH) RNA-binding domain.
source: ketu is a missense mutation in Ythdc2 (YTH-domain containing 2), which encodes a protein with RNA helicase motifs and a YT521-B homology (YTH) RNA-binding domain (Stoilov et al., 2002; Morohashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Stoilov et al., 2002 and Morohashi et al., 2011, as well as domain analysis in the manuscript (Figure 8).

claim: Recombinant YTHDC2 protein displays 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity.
source: Recombinant YTHDC2 protein displays 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity and a solution structure of its YTH domain is consistent with direct recognition of N6-methyladenosine-containing RNA.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by biochemical assays (Figure 9).

claim: A solution structure of the YTHDC2 YTH domain is consistent with direct recognition of N6-methyladenosine-containing RNA.
source: Recombinant YTHDC2 protein displays 3′→5′ RNA helicase activity and a solution structure of its YTH domain is consistent with direct recognition of N6-methyladenosine-containing RNA.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by structural analysis (Figure 8).

claim: Ythdc2ketu homozygotes are both male- and female-sterile.
source: Ythdc2ketu homozygotes are both male- and female-sterile.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data and histological analysis (Figure 3).

claim: In the testis, mutant germ cells carry out an abortive attempt at meiosis: they express hallmark meiotic proteins and initiate recombination, but fail to fully extinguish the spermatogonial mitotic division program, proceed prematurely to an aberrant metaphase-like state, and undergo apoptosis.
source: In the testis, mutant germ cells carry out an abortive attempt at meiosis: they express hallmark meiotic proteins and initiate recombination, but fail to fully extinguish the spermatogonial mitotic division program, proceed prematurely to an aberrant metaphase-like state, and undergo apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence, histological, and TUNEL data (Figures 1, 3, 4, 5).

claim: The ketu phenotype is similar to mutants lacking MEIOC.
source: This phenotype is similar to mutants lacking MEIOC, a meiosis-specific protein that was recently shown to be a binding partner of YTHDC2 and that has been proposed to regulate male and female meiosis by controlling the stability of various mRNAs (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by comparison of phenotypes and citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: MEIOC is a meiosis-specific protein that was recently shown to be a binding partner of YTHDC2.
source: This phenotype is similar to mutants lacking MEIOC, a meiosis-specific protein that was recently shown to be a binding partner of YTHDC2 and that has been proposed to regulate male and female meiosis by controlling the stability of various mRNAs (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: MEIOC has been proposed to regulate male and female meiosis by controlling the stability of various mRNAs.
source: This phenotype is similar to mutants lacking MEIOC, a meiosis-specific protein that was recently shown to be a binding partner of YTHDC2 and that has been proposed to regulate male and female meiosis by controlling the stability of various mRNAs (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: YTHDC2 has an essential role in the germlines of male and female mice.
source: Our results thus reveal an essential role for YTHDC2 in the germlines of male and female mice and show that YTHDC2 is an indispensable functional partner of MEIOC.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the sterility phenotype of Ythdc2 mutants in both sexes (Figure 3).

claim: YTHDC2 is an indispensable functional partner of MEIOC.
source: Our results thus reveal an essential role for YTHDC2 in the germlines of male and female mice and show that YTHDC2 is an indispensable functional partner of MEIOC.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the similar phenotypes of Ythdc2 and Meioc mutants.

claim: The YTHDC2-MEIOC complex is an evolutionarily ancient factor, present in the last common ancestor (LCA) of Metazoa.
source: Furthermore, phylogenetic studies demonstrate that the YTHDC2-MEIOC complex is an evolutionarily ancient factor, present in the last common ancestor (LCA) of Metazoa.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing conservation across metazoans (Figures 10, 11).

claim: Despite high conservation in most metazoans, there are unexpectedly complex evolutionary patterns for YTHDC2 and MEIOC family members in specific lineages, particularly nematodes and the Schizophora section of flies.
source: Nevertheless, despite high conservation in most metazoans, we uncover unexpectedly complex evolutionary patterns for YTHDC2 and MEIOC family members in specific lineages, particularly nematodes and the Schizophora section of flies, which includes Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figures 10, 11).

claim: Mutagenesis was performed by treatment of male mice of the C57BL/6J strain with the alkylating agent N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea (ENU).
source: Mutagenesis was performed by treatment of male mice of the C57BL/6J strain (B6 hereafter) with the alkylating agent N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea (ENU).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: ENU introduces de novo mutations in the germline, predominantly single base substitutions.
source: ENU introduces de novo mutations in the germline, predominantly single base substitutions (Hitotsumachi et al., 1985; Caspary and Anderson, 2006; Probst and Justice, 2010).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Hitotsumachi et al., 1985, Caspary and Anderson, 2006, and Probst and Justice, 2010.

claim: A three-generation breeding scheme including outcrossing with females of the FVB/NJ strain was followed to uncover recessive mutations causing defects in male meiosis.
source: To uncover recessive mutations causing defects in male meiosis, we followed a three-generation breeding scheme including outcrossing with females of the FVB/NJ strain (FVB hereafter) (Caspary and Anderson, 2006; Caspary, 2010; Jain et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and illustrated in Figure 1A, with citations to Caspary and Anderson, 2006, Caspary, 2010, and Jain et al., 2017.

claim: In the ketu line, 5 of 26 G3 males screened contained SYCP3-positive spermatocytes displaying extreme meiotic defects, with no cells resembling normal meiotic prophase I stages.
source: In an F1 founder line we named ketu, 5 of 26 G3 males screened (Figure 1C) contained SYCP3-positive spermatocytes displaying extreme meiotic defects, with no cells resembling normal meiotic prophase I stages (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by data in Figures 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: Type I cells displayed few or none of the normal dots or lines of SYCP3 staining typical of early stages of axial element formation in leptonema and accounted for 74% to 88% of cells.
source: Type I cells displayed few or none of the normal dots or lines of SYCP3 staining typical of early stages of axial element formation in leptonema; this was the most abundant class, accounting for 74% to 88% of cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: Type II cells displayed prominent dots or short lines of SYCP3 and accounted for 12% to 25% of cells.
source: Type II cells displayed prominent dots or short lines of SYCP3; these accounted for 12% to 25% of cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: Type III cells had numerous longer lines of SYCP3, consistent with more advanced axial element formation, and were rare in the younger animals screened (<0.6%) but accumulated to slightly higher levels (3%) in the older G3 animal screened.
source: Type III cells had numerous longer lines of SYCP3, consistent with more advanced axial element formation; these were rare in the younger animals screened (<0.6%) but accumulated to slightly higher levels (3%) in the older G3 animal screened (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: All three cell types had prominent aggregates of SYCP3 and pan-nuclear γH2AX staining.
source: All three cell types had prominent aggregates of SYCP3 and pan-nuclear γH2AX staining (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1B.

claim: The strong γH2AX staining is consistent with these cells having initiated meiotic recombination via formation of double-strand breaks by SPO11.
source: The strong γH2AX staining is consistent with these cells having initiated meiotic recombination via formation of double-strand breaks by SPO11 (Baudat et al., 2000; Mahadevaiah et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Baudat et al., 2000 and Mahadevaiah et al., 2001, as well as inference from the γH2AX staining pattern.

claim: ketu mutant spermatocytes formed numerous foci of the meiosis-specific strand exchange protein DMC1.
source: Supporting this interpretation, immunostaining demonstrated that ketu mutant spermatocytes formed numerous foci of the meiosis-specific strand exchange protein DMC1 (Bishop et al., 1992; Tarsounas et al., 1999) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1E, with citations to Bishop et al., 1992 and Tarsounas et al., 1999.

claim: The ketu mutation is an A to G nucleotide transition at position Chr18:44840277, resulting in a missense mutation in predicted exon 6.
source: This variant is an A to G nucleotide transition at position Chr18:44840277, resulting in a missense mutation in predicted exon 6 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequencing data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The ketu mutation changes codon 327 (CAT, histidine) to CGT (arginine), altering a highly conserved residue adjacent to the DEVH box.
source: The mutation changes codon 327 (CAT, histidine) to CGT (arginine), altering a highly conserved residue adjacent to the DEVH box (described in more detail below).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence analysis (Figure 2C and Figure 8B).

claim: Ythdc2 mRNA is expressed in adult testes as well as widely in other adult and embryonic tissues.
source: Ythdc2 mRNA is expressed in adult testes as well as widely in other adult and embryonic tissues (Figure 2B,D), thus placing Ythdc2 expression at an appropriate time to contribute to spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by ENCODE RNA-seq data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: YTHDC2 protein was reported to interact in vivo with the meiosis-specific MEIOC protein, which is itself required for meiosis.
source: While this work was in progress, YTHDC2 protein was reported to interact in vivo with the meiosis-specific MEIOC protein, which is itself required for meiosis (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: A CRISPR/Cas9-induced frameshift mutation in exon 2 of Ythdc2 failed to complement the ketu mutation.
source: Furthermore, a CRISPR/Cas9-induced frameshift mutation in exon 2 of Ythdc2 (Figure 2B,C) failed to complement the ketu mutation (see below).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by complementation data and the description of the em1 allele (Figure 2B,C and Figure 3).

claim: Ythdc2ketu/+ heterozygotes had normal fertility and transmitted the mutation in a Mendelian ratio.
source: Ythdc2ketu/+ heterozygotes had normal fertility and transmitted the mutation in a Mendelian ratio (30.8% Ythdc2+/+, 46.6% Ythdc2ketu/+, and 22.6% Ythdc2ketu/ketu from heterozygote × heterozygote crosses; n = 305 mice; p=0.28, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data and statistical analysis.

claim: No obvious somatic defects were observed by gross histopathological analysis of major organs and tissues of adult Ythdc2ketu/ketu mice.
source: No obvious somatic defects were observed by gross histopathological analysis of major organs and tissues of adult Ythdc2ketu/ketu mice (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histopathological examination described in Materials and methods.

claim: Ythdc2ketu/ketu homozygous males were sterile: none of the three animals tested sired progeny when bred with wild-type females for 8 weeks.
source: However, Ythdc2ketu/ketu homozygous males were sterile: none of the three animals tested sired progeny when bred with wild-type females for 8 weeks.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data.

claim: Mutant males showed a 76.4% reduction in testes-to-body-weight ratio compared to littermates.
source: Mutant males showed a 76.4% reduction in testes-to-body-weight ratio compared to littermates (mean ratios were 0.14% for Ythdc2ketu/ketu and 0.58% for wild-type and heterozygous animals; p<0.01, one-sided t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative data in Figure 3A.

claim: In histological sections of adult testes, seminiferous tubules from Ythdc2ketu/ketu males were greatly reduced in diameter and contained only Sertoli cells and early spermatogenic cells, with no post-meiotic germ cells.
source: In histological sections of adult testes, seminiferous tubules from Ythdc2ketu/ketu males were greatly reduced in diameter and contained only Sertoli cells and early spermatogenic cells, with no post-meiotic germ cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figure 3B.

claim: At 8 dpp, most wild-type tubules contained only spermatogonia and Sertoli cells, and no defects were apparent in Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants compared to normal littermate controls.
source: At 8 dpp, most wild-type tubules contained only spermatogonia and Sertoli cells, as expected, and no defects were apparent in Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants compared to normal littermate controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figure 3C.

claim: At 10 dpp, testis sections from Ythdc2ketu/ketu mice had a few tubules containing germ cells with abnormal morphology in which the chromosomes were condensed and individualized, reminiscent of metaphase rather than prophase.
source: At the same age, testis sections from Ythdc2ketu/ketu mice also had a mix of tubules at slightly different stages, but a few tubules (labeled 'Ab' in Figure 3C) contained germ cells with abnormal morphology in which the chromosomes were condensed and individualized (arrowheads in Figure 3C), reminiscent of metaphase rather than prophase.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figure 3C.

claim: At 10 dpp in normal animals, no spermatocytes are expected to have reached even zygonema, let alone to have exited prophase.
source: At this age in normal animals, no spermatocytes are expected to have reached even zygonema, let alone to have exited prophase (Bellvé et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Bellvé et al., 1977.

claim: By 14 dpp, essentially all tubules in wild type had germ cells in meiotic prophase, but Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants displayed a mix of tubule types.
source: By 14 dpp, essentially all tubules in wild type had germ cells in meiotic prophase, but Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants displayed a mix of tubule types: some tubules ('Ab' in Figure 3C) had normal looking germ cells along with cells with metaphase-like chromosomes, and often contained cells with highly compacted, presumably apoptotic nuclei as well; and some had only a single layer of cells (spermatogonia plus Sertoli cells) along the tubule perimeter ('Ep' in Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: TUNEL staining demonstrated a substantially higher incidence of apoptosis at 14 and 15 dpp in the Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, TUNEL staining demonstrated a substantially higher incidence of apoptosis at 14 and 15 dpp in the Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant compared to wild type (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated apoptosis was also observed at 10 dpp, but not in every littermate pair of this age, presumably reflecting animal-to-animal differences in developmental timing.
source: Elevated apoptosis was also observed at 10 dpp, but not in every littermate pair of this age, presumably reflecting animal-to-animal differences in developmental timing (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see also RNA-seq section below).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No increase in apoptosis was observed for Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants at 8 dpp.
source: No increase in apoptosis was observed for Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants at 8 dpp (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ythdc2ketu/ketu spermatogonia are able to proliferate mitotically but then transition to an aberrant state in which chromosomes condense prematurely and apoptosis is triggered.
source: We conclude that Ythdc2ketu/ketu spermatogonia are able to proliferate mitotically but then transition to an aberrant state in which chromosomes condense prematurely and apoptosis is triggered.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by the histological and TUNEL data (Figure 3).

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 and a guide RNA targeted to exon 2 were used to generate an endonuclease-mediated (em) allele containing a 5 bp deletion plus 1 bp insertion, resulting in a frameshift.
source: To verify that the Ythdc2 point mutation in the ketu line is causative for the spermatogenesis defect, we used CRISPR/Cas9 and a guide RNA targeted to exon 2 to generate an endonuclease-mediated (em) allele containing a 5 bp deletion plus 1 bp insertion, resulting in a frameshift (Figure 2B,C) (Ythdc2em1Sky, hereafter Ythdc2em1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the description of the em1 allele in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Ythdc2em1/+ heterozygotes transmitted the mutation in a Mendelian ratio.
source: Ythdc2em1/+ heterozygotes transmitted the mutation in a Mendelian ratio (30.7% Ythdc2+/+, 48.5% Ythdc2em1/+, and 20.8% Ythdc2em1/em1; n = 101 mice; p=0.62, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data and statistical analysis.

claim: Ythdc2em1/em1 homozygotes displayed hypogonadism and altered testis histology indistinguishable from Ythdc2ketu/ketu homozygotes, including the appearance of cells with abnormally condensed chromosomes.
source: Indeed, Ythdc2em1/em1 homozygotes displayed hypogonadism (0.19% mean testes-to-body-weight ratio for Ythdc2em1/em1 and 0.57% for wild-type and heterozygous animals; 66.8% reduction; p<0.01, one-sided t-test) and altered testis histology indistinguishable from Ythdc2ketu/ketu homozygotes, including the appearance of cells with abnormally condensed chromosomes (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative and histological data in Figures 3A and 3E.

claim: Ythdc2em1/em1 males were sterile.
source: Moreover, Ythdc2em1/em1 males were sterile (none of the three animals tested sired progeny when bred with wild-type females for 8–9 weeks).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data.

claim: Ythdc2ketu/em1 compound heterozygotes were equally defective and sterile.
source: Ythdc2ketu/em1 compound heterozygotes were equally defective (0.20% mean testes-to-body-weight ratio for Ythdc2ketu/em1 and 0.63% for wild-type and single-heterozygous animals; 67.5% reduction; p<0.01, one-sided t-test) (Figure 3A,F) and sterile (two animals tested did not sire progeny when bred with wild-type females for 9 weeks).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative data in Figures 3A and 3F, and breeding data.

claim: ketu is allelic to Ythdc2em1.
source: Thus, ketu is allelic to Ythdc2em1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by the complementation test showing that ketu/em1 compound heterozygotes are defective.

claim: Ythdc2ketu/ketu females were sterile: no pregnancies were observed from crosses of 5 homozygous mutant females to wild-type males.
source: Ythdc2ketu/ketu females were also sterile: no pregnancies were observed from crosses of 5 homozygous mutant females to wild-type males (bred for 6–19 weeks).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by breeding data.

claim: Ovaries from Ythdc2ketu/ketu females were dramatically smaller compared to wild-type littermates, and no developing follicles were visible in adults.
source: Ovaries from Ythdc2ketu/ketu females were dramatically smaller compared to wild-type littermates, and no developing follicles were visible in adults (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Ythdc2em1/em1 homozygotes displayed the same phenotype as Ythdc2ketu/ketu females.
source: Again, Ythdc2em1/em1 homozygotes displayed the same phenotype as Ythdc2ketu/ketu females (Figure 3G,H) and no pregnancies were observed from crosses of 3 homozygous mutant females to wild-type males (bred for 9–21 weeks).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by histological data in Figures 3G and 3H, and breeding data.

claim: In mice homozygous for a targeted Meioc mutation, male and female germ cells enter meiosis at the correct developmental stage but show substantial meiotic defects including rapid progression to a metaphase-like state with condensed univalent chromosomes and monopolar spindles.
source: In mice homozygous for a targeted Meioc mutation, male and female germ cells enter meiosis at the correct developmental stage (i.e., in juvenile males around 10 dpp, and in fetal ovary around embryonic day 14.5), but show substantial meiotic defects including rapid progression to a metaphase-like state with condensed univalent chromosomes and monopolar spindles (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: In wild type, groups of mitotic spermatogonia were observed in which strong pH3 staining coated condensed chromosomes that were aligned on a metaphase plate with a bipolar spindle and pericentromeric heterochromatin clustered near the middle of the metaphase plate.
source: In wild type, we observed groups of mitotic spermatogonia in which strong pH3 staining coated condensed chromosomes that were aligned on a metaphase plate with a bipolar spindle and pericentromeric heterochromatin (DAPI-bright regions) clustered near the middle of the metaphase plate (Figure 4A,B,D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 4A, 4B, 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No spermatocytes with pH3-positive, condensed chromosomes were observed in wild type, as expected because wild-type germ cells do not reach the first meiotic division until ~18 dpp.
source: No spermatocytes with pH3-positive, condensed chromosomes were observed, as expected because wild-type germ cells do not reach the first meiotic division until ~18 dpp (Bellvé et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Bellvé et al., 1977.

claim: In Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants, cells with condensed, strongly pH3-positive chromosomes were ~6 fold more abundant.
source: In Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants in contrast, cells with condensed, strongly pH3-positive chromosomes were ~6 fold more abundant (Figure 4A,C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, p<0.01 comparing percent of strongly pH3-positive cells with DAPI staining indicative of condensed chromatin in juvenile wild type and mutant animals (t-test)).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figures 4A, 4C, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Most pH3-positive cells in Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants were spermatocytes as judged by their more lumenal position within the tubules and the presence of SYCP3 at centromeres on chromosome spreads.
source: More importantly, unlike in wild type, most of these cells were spermatocytes as judged by their more lumenal position within the tubules (Figure 4A,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and the presence of SYCP3 at centromeres on chromosome spreads (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 4A, 4C, 4F, 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In most spermatocytes in Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants, the mass of condensed chromosomes had microtubules forming a single visible aster.
source: Moreover, in most of these spermatocytes the mass of condensed chromosomes had microtubules forming a single visible aster (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 4C and 4E.

claim: Wild-type meiosis during metaphase I showed the expected bipolar α-tubulin-containing spindles and well-aligned chromosomes at mid-spindle, with pericentromeric heterochromatin at the outer edges of the metaphase plate and oriented toward the poles.
source: These apparently monopolar spindles contrasted starkly with those in wild-type meiosis during metaphase I (visualized in adult testes), which showed the expected bipolar α-tubulin-containing spindles and well-aligned chromosomes at mid-spindle, with pericentromeric heterochromatin at the outer edges of the metaphase plate and oriented toward the poles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant and controls had similar numbers of BrdU+ cells, inferred to be replicating spermatogonia and cells that have undergone pre-meiotic replication.
source: As expected, the mutant and controls had similar numbers of BrdU+ cells, inferred to be replicating spermatogonia and cells that have undergone pre-meiotic replication (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, p=0.54 in t-test comparing percent of BrdU+ cells in wild type/heterozygous and mutant).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figures 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BrdU+ SYCP3+ double-positive cells were observed in the Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant at a frequency comparable to the controls.
source: Importantly, however, BrdU+ SYCP3+ double-positive cells were observed in the mutant at a frequency comparable to the controls (Figure 5C, p=0.03 comparing percent of SYCP3+ cells in wild type/heterozygous and mutant, and p=0.53 comparing percent of double-positive cells (t-test)).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: The presence of presumptive pre-leptotene spermatocytes suggests that pre-meiotic DNA replication occurs in a timely manner in the Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant, similar to Meioc–/–, although modest defects in timing or efficiency cannot be ruled out.
source: The presence of these presumptive pre-leptotene spermatocytes suggests that pre-meiotic DNA replication occurs in a timely manner in the Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutant, similar to Meioc–/– (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017), although modest defects in timing or efficiency cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the BrdU/SYCP3 double-positive cell data, with citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: In normal spermatogenesis, cyclin A2 (CCNA2) is expressed during mitotic cell cycles in spermatogonia, but is downregulated at or before meiotic entry and is undetectable in SYCP3-positive spermatocytes.
source: In normal spermatogenesis, cyclin A2 (CCNA2) is expressed during mitotic cell cycles in spermatogonia, but is downregulated at or before meiotic entry and is undetectable in SYCP3-positive spermatocytes (Ravnik and Wolgemuth, 1999).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Ravnik and Wolgemuth, 1999.

claim: Meioc–/– spermatocytes fail to properly extinguish CCNA2 expression, suggesting that inappropriate retention of the spermatogonial (mitotic) cell cycle machinery contributes to precocious metaphase and other meiotic defects.
source: Meioc–/– spermatocytes fail to properly extinguish CCNA2 expression, suggesting that inappropriate retention of the spermatogonial (mitotic) cell cycle machinery contributes to precocious metaphase and other meiotic defects (Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Soh et al., 2017.

claim: In testis sections from 12-, 14-, and 15-dpp wild-type animals, the expected mutually exclusive localization pattern of CCNA2 and SYCP3 was observed: CCNA2+ spermatogonia were located at tubule peripheries while SYCP3+ spermatocytes occupied more lumenal positions, and double-positive cells were rare.
source: When testis sections from 12-, 14-, and 15-dpp wild-type animals were immunostained for SYCP3 and CCNA2, the expected mutually exclusive localization pattern was observed: CCNA2+ spermatogonia were located at tubule peripheries while SYCP3+ spermatocytes occupied more lumenal positions (Figure 5D, left), and double-positive cells were rare (Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5D, 5E, 5F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In testis sections from Ythdc2ketu/ketu animals of the same ages, a substantial fraction of SYCP3+ spermatocytes also contained nuclear CCNA2.
source: In testis sections from Ythdc2ketu/ketu animals of the same ages, however, a substantial fraction of SYCP3+ spermatocytes also contained nuclear CCNA2 (Figure 5D, right, Figure 5E,F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5D, 5E, 5F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Ythdc2 mutant showed a net increase in the number of CCNA2+ cells, and much of this increase can be attributed to cells that initiated a meiotic program (i.e., were SYCP3+), but a small increase in the spermatogonial pool cannot be ruled out.
source: Indeed, the Ythdc2 mutant showed a net increase in the number of CCNA2+ cells, and much of this increase can be attributed to cells that initiated a meiotic program (i.e., were SYCP3+), but a small increase in the spermatogonial pool cannot be ruled out (Figure 5F, p<0.01 comparing wild type and mutant animals for percent of SYCP3+ cells, or CCNA2+ cells, or double-positive cells (t-test)).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F.

claim: Ythdc2-defective germ cells make an abortive attempt to enter meiosis but fail to fully extinguish the spermatogonial program, progress precociously to a metaphase-like state, and undergo apoptosis.
source: Collectively, these data lead us to conclude that Ythdc2-defective germ cells make an abortive attempt to enter meiosis but fail to fully extinguish the spermatogonial program, progress precociously to a metaphase-like state, and undergo apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by the immunofluorescence, histological, and TUNEL data (Figures 3, 4, 5).

claim: The Ythdc2 and Meioc mutant phenotypes are highly concordant, supporting the hypothesis that YTHDC2 and MEIOC function together to regulate germ cell development around the time of meiotic entry.
source: The Ythdc2 and Meioc mutant phenotypes are highly concordant in this regard (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017), supporting the hypothesis that YTHDC2 and MEIOC function together to regulate germ cell development around the time of meiotic entry.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by comparison of phenotypes and citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: RNA sequencing was performed on whole testes from Ythdc2em1/em1 and wild-type or heterozygous littermate controls at 8, 9, and 10 dpp.
source: To test whether the deregulation of meiotic progression in the absence of YTHDC2 was accompanied by alterations in the transcriptome, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on whole testes from Ythdc2em1/em1 and wild-type or heterozygous littermate controls. We analyzed steady-state RNA levels at 8 and 9 dpp, at or slightly before initiation of meiosis, and at 10 dpp, by which time aberrant metaphases were observed in the mutant (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 6.

claim: At 8 and 9 dpp, only small numbers of genes (a dozen or fewer) scored as significantly up- or downregulated in the mutants at a modestly stringent statistical cutoff (adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: At a modestly stringent statistical cutoff (adjusted p-value<0.05), only small numbers of genes (a dozen or fewer) scored as significantly up- or downregulated in the mutants at 8 and 9 dpp (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 10 dpp, a similarly small number of genes were upregulated, but a larger group (69 genes) was significantly downregulated.
source: At 10 dpp, a similarly small number of genes were upregulated, but a larger group (69 genes) was significantly downregulated (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cluster I comprised genes whose expression remained low during these time points in wild type but were generally upregulated in Ythdc2em1/em1 mutants.
source: Cluster I comprised genes whose expression remained low during these time points in wild type but were generally upregulated in Ythdc2em1/em1 mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Clusters II and III comprised genes whose expression in wild type rose sharply between 9 and 10 dpp but that mostly failed to increase in mutants.
source: Clusters II and III comprised genes whose expression in wild type rose sharply between 9 and 10 dpp but that mostly failed to increase in mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cluster IV comprised genes whose expression in wild type increased more gradually or remained high over this period but that remained consistently lower in mutants.
source: And Cluster IV comprised genes whose expression in wild type increased more gradually or remained high over this period but that remained consistently lower in mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cluster I was enriched for genes whose expression was higher in sorted spermatogonia compared to spermatocytes.
source: Cluster I was enriched for genes whose expression was higher in sorted spermatogonia compared to spermatocytes (p<0.0001; paired t-test), while Clusters II and III were enriched for genes with the opposite developmental pattern (p<0.01).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by comparison to published RNA-seq data from sorted testis cell populations (Figure 6C).

claim: Clusters II and III were enriched for genes with expression higher in spermatocytes compared to spermatogonia.
source: Cluster I was enriched for genes whose expression was higher in sorted spermatogonia compared to spermatocytes (p<0.0001; paired t-test), while Clusters II and III were enriched for genes with the opposite developmental pattern (p<0.01).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by comparison to published RNA-seq data from sorted testis cell populations (Figure 6C).

claim: Clusters II and III were highly enriched for meiosis-related gene ontology (GO) terms.
source: Furthermore, Clusters II and III were highly enriched for meiosis-related gene ontology (GO) terms (adjusted p-value<0.05, Figure 6D; Clusters I and IV were not significantly enriched for any GO terms).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Genes destined to increase over time in wild type tended to be expressed at lower levels in mutants at 8 dpp, while genes that should be destined to decrease over time tended to be overexpressed in the mutant.
source: Strikingly, when subdivided according to developmental fate in wild type, these genes showed opposing behaviors in mutants at 8 dpp: the genes that would be destined to increase over time in wild type tended to be expressed at lower levels in mutants at 8 dpp, while genes that should be destined to decrease over time tended to be overexpressed in the mutant (Figure 6E; p=2.6×10−244 comparing the two developmentally regulated groups).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ccna2 transcript levels declined over the time points examined in wild type, but went down to a lesser degree at 10 dpp in mutants.
source: Ccna2 transcript levels declined over the time points examined in wild type, but went down to a lesser degree at 10 dpp in mutants. Although this difference was not large enough to meet our cutoff for statistical significance (log2 fold change at 10 dpp = 0.23 with adjusted p-value=0.26), it is consistent with the observed persistence of CCNA2 protein expression (Figure 5D,F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The transcript level of Ccnb3, encoding a meiotic cyclin expressed during early prophase I, was decreased at 10 dpp in mutants compared to wild type.
source: In comparison, the transcript level of Ccnb3, encoding a meiotic cyclin expressed during early prophase I (Nguyen et al., 2002), was decreased at 10 dpp in mutants compared to wild type (log2 fold change at 10 dpp = −1.60 with adjusted p-value<0.01), as were transcripts for other canonical meiotic genes Sycp3, Dmc1, Spo11, and Msh5 (log2 fold changes at 10 dpp = −0.42, −0.46, −1.97, −1.05, respectively; adjusted p-value<0.01 for Sycp3, Spo11, Msh5, and 0.06 for Dmc1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6F, with citation to Nguyen et al., 2002.

claim: Ythdc2 transcripts were decreased in mutants at all ages examined, most likely reflecting nonsense-mediated decay caused by the frameshift mutation.
source: Ythdc2 transcripts were decreased in mutants at all ages examined (log2 fold change at 8, 9, 10 dpp = −2.50, −2.52, −2.42, respectively, with adjusted p-value<0.01), most likely reflecting nonsense-mediated decay caused by the frameshift mutation.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Meioc was unaffected during this developmental window.
source: Meioc was unaffected during this developmental window (log2 fold change at 8, 9, 10 dpp = −1.02, −0.10, −0.12, respectively, with adjusted p-value=1.0).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: YTHDC2 is important for the developmental transition from a spermatogonial to a meiotic gene expression program and RNA changes appear before overt morphological changes or cellular attrition through programmed cell death occur.
source: Collectively, these findings support the conclusion that YTHDC2 is important for the developmental transition from a spermatogonial to a meiotic gene expression program and that RNA changes appear before overt morphological changes or cellular attrition through programmed cell death occur.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by the RNA-seq data (Figure 6) and comparison with histological and TUNEL data (Figure 3).

claim: The influence of YTHDC2 on transcript abundance (whether direct or indirect) is quantitatively modest and can vary substantially in direction between affected transcripts.
source: However, we emphasize that the influence of YTHDC2 on transcript abundance (whether direct or indirect) is quantitatively modest and can vary substantially in direction between affected transcripts.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 6).

claim: Decreased levels of meiotic transcripts were also observed in microarray analyses of 8-dpp Meioc–/– testes.
source: Decreased levels of meiotic transcripts were also observed in microarray analyses of 8-dpp Meioc–/– testes (Abby et al., 2016), and a similar overall pattern of downregulated meiotic genes and/or upregulated mitotic genes was seen with microarray or RNA-seq data from Meioc–/– ovaries at embryonic day 14.5 (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: YTHDC2 staining was prominent in SYCP3-positive spermatocytes in wild type, whereas little to no staining was observed in spermatocytes from Ythdc2em1/em1 littermates.
source: YTHDC2 staining was prominent in SYCP3-positive spermatocytes in wild type, whereas little to no staining was observed in spermatocytes from Ythdc2em1/em1 littermates (Figure 7A), validating antibody specificity.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7A.

claim: Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants displayed only background levels of YTHDC2 staining in SYCP3-positive cells, similar to Ythdc2em1/em1 mutants.
source: In contrast to wild-type littermates, Ythdc2ketu/ketu mutants displayed only background levels of YTHDC2 staining in SYCP3-positive cells (arrowheads in Figure 7B), similar to Ythdc2em1/em1 mutants.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B.

claim: The Ythdc2ketu mutation may destabilize the protein, and/or YTHDC2 may be required (directly or indirectly) for its own expression as cells transition into meiosis.
source: The Ythdc2ketu mutation may destabilize the protein, and/or YTHDC2 may be required (directly or indirectly) for its own expression as cells transition into meiosis (discussed further below).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of reduced YTHDC2 protein levels in ketu mutants.

claim: No YTHDC2 staining above background was observed in spermatogonia or Sertoli cells in wild type.
source: In wild type, no YTHDC2 staining above background was observed in spermatogonia or Sertoli cells (e.g., exemplified by the stage I–III tubule in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7C.

claim: Strong YTHDC2 staining first became detectable in pre-leptotene spermatocytes, remained strong from leptonema through diplonema, then returned to background levels in postmeiotic cells (round spermatids).
source: Strong staining first became detectable in pre-leptotene spermatocytes (stage VIII tubule, Figure 7C), remained strong from leptonema through diplonema, then returned to background levels in postmeiotic cells (round spermatids) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7C.

claim: YTHDC2 appeared cytoplasmic throughout prophase I, with no detectable nuclear signal above background.
source: YTHDC2 appeared cytoplasmic throughout prophase I, with no detectable nuclear signal above background.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7C.

claim: The predicted Ythdc2 transcript encodes a protein of 1445 amino acids and 161 kDa.
source: The predicted Ythdc2 transcript encodes a protein of 1445 amino acids and 161 kDa (presented schematically in Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the schematic in Figure 8A.

claim: Protein domains and amino acid sequence motifs characteristic of superfamily 2 DExH-box helicases are conserved in mouse YTHDC2 and its homologs throughout Eumetazoa.
source: Protein domains and amino acid sequence motifs characteristic of superfamily 2 DExH-box helicases are conserved in mouse YTHDC2 and its homologs throughout Eumetazoa (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by domain analysis and sequence alignments in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: YTHDC2 is predicted to have the helicase core modules (DEXDc and HELICc domains, including matches to helicase conserved sequence motifs) and two C-terminal extensions (the helicase-associated 2 (HA2) and oligonucleotide binding (OB) domains) that are characteristic of the DEAH/RNA helicase A (RHA) helicase family.
source: More specifically, YTHDC2 is predicted to have the helicase core modules (DEXDc and HELICc domains, including matches to helicase conserved sequence motifs) and two C-terminal extensions (the helicase-associated 2 (HA2) and oligonucleotide binding (OB) domains) that are characteristic of the DEAH/RNA helicase A (RHA) helicase family (Figure 8A,B and Supplementary file 2) (Fairman-Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by domain analysis in Figures 8A and 8B, with citation to Fairman-Williams et al., 2010.

claim: The ketu mutation (H327R) alters the amino acid located four residues N-terminal of the DEVH sequence.
source: The ketu mutation (H327R) alters the amino acid located four residues N-terminal of the DEVH sequence (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 8B.

claim: The histidine at position 327 is invariant across likely YTHDC2 orthologs.
source: This histidine is invariant across likely YTHDC2 orthologs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 8B.

claim: The YTH domain of human YTHDC2 adopts an open α/β fold with a core composed of six β strands surrounded by four alpha helices.
source: The YTHDC2 YTH domain adopts an open α/β fold with a core composed of six β strands surrounded by four alpha helices.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The YTHDC2 YTH domain solution structure matched closely with the crystal structure of RNA-bound YTHDC1 (Cα r.m.s.d. = 2.27 Å) and the conserved m6A-binding residues aligned well.
source: This solution structure matched closely with the crystal structure of RNA-bound YTHDC1 (Cα r.m.s.d. = 2.27 Å) and, importantly, the conserved m6A-binding residues aligned well (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by structural superposition shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The human YTHDC2 YTH domain was reported to bind m6A-modified RNAs, albeit with substantially weaker affinity than YTH domains from other proteins.
source: Consistent with this structural conservation, the human YTHDC2 YTH domain was reported to bind m6A-modified RNAs, albeit with substantially weaker affinity than YTH domains from other proteins (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: The Mmi1 YTH domain binds a specific RNA sequence called a 'determinant of selective removal' (DSR: 5′-UNAAA/C) found in transcripts of meiotic and other genes.
source: The YTH domain of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe Mmi1 protein is an exception to the more widely found m6A-binding specificity. Rather than binding m6A, the Mmi1 YTH domain binds a specific RNA sequence called a 'determinant of selective removal' (DSR: 5′-UNAAA/C) found in transcripts of meiotic and other genes (Harigaya et al., 2006; Yamashita et al., 2012; Chatterjee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Harigaya et al., 2006, Yamashita et al., 2012, and Chatterjee et al., 2016.

claim: Several key residues involved in DSR binding are not conserved in mouse and human YTHDC2.
source: Although the human YTHDC2 structure superimposes well on that of Mmi1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), several key residues involved in DSR binding are not conserved in mouse and human YTHDC2 (red boxes in Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 8D and structural comparison in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: It is unlikely that the YTH domain of YTHDC2 utilizes the DSR interaction surface to bind RNA.
source: We infer that it is unlikely that the YTH domain of YTHDC2 utilizes the DSR interaction surface to bind RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of conservation of key DSR-binding residues in YTHDC2.

claim: YTHDC2 has RNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
source: YTHDC2 has been shown to have RNA-stimulated ATPase activity (Morohashi et al., 2011) and was sometimes referred to as an RNA helicase (e.g.,Tanabe et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017), but direct demonstration of helicase activity had not yet been reported at the time our studies were conducted.
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Morohashi et al., 2011.

claim: Unwinding was observed for the 3' tailed substrates but not for substrates with blunt ends or 5' overhangs, indicating a 3′→5' helicase activity.
source: Unwinding was observed for the 3' tailed substrates but not for substrates with blunt ends or 5' overhangs (Figure 9B), indicating a 3′→5' helicase activity.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by biochemical assay data in Figure 9B.

claim: ATP was required for duplex unwinding.
source: ATP was required for duplex unwinding (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by biochemical assay data in Figure 9C.

claim: YTHDC2 was more active on duplexes with a 3' poly(U) overhang than a 3' poly(A) overhang.
source: Under these conditions, YTHDC2 was more active on duplexes with a 3' poly(U) overhang than a 3' poly(A) overhang (Figure 9B), and at a set enzyme concentration, it unwound the 3' poly(U) overhang substrate more efficiently (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by biochemical assay data in Figures 9B, 9D, and 9E.

claim: Introduction of the ketu mutation in YTHDC2 led to protein insolubility when expressed in insect cells.
source: Introduction of the ketu mutation in YTHDC2 led to protein insolubilty when expressed in insect cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by protein expression data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Purified MBP-tagged YTHDC2H327R showed a modest reduction of specific activity in the RNA unwinding assay.
source: Purified MBP-tagged YTHDC2H327R showed a modest reduction of specific activity in the RNA unwinding assay (Figure 9F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by biochemical assay data in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: It is likely that functional inactivation caused by the H327R substitution is a consequence of misfolding or protein aggregation, which would be consistent with the observed decrease in protein levels in vivo.
source: Thus, it is likely that functional inactivation caused by the H327R substitution is a consequence of misfolding or protein aggregation, which would be consistent with the observed decrease in protein levels in vivo (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a likely explanation based on the insolubility of the mutant protein and reduced protein levels in vivo.

claim: YTHDC2 homologs were found in metazoan species in a limited analysis of conservation.
source: YTHDC2 homologs were found in metazoan species in a limited analysis of conservation (Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Soh et al., 2017.

claim: The closest homolog of YTHDC2 in Drosophila melanogaster is Bgcn (benign gonial cell neoplasm), which regulates germ cell differentiation via translational control of target mRNAs.
source: The closest homolog in Drosophila melanogaster is Bgcn (benign gonial cell neoplasm), which regulates germ cell differentiation via translational control of target mRNAs (Li et al., 2009b; Kim et al., 2010; Insco et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Li et al., 2009b, Kim et al., 2010, Insco et al., 2012, and Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Bgcn was proposed to be the fruit fly ortholog of YTHDC2.
source: Bgcn was thus proposed to be the fruit fly ortholog of YTHDC2 (Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Soh et al., 2017.

claim: Bgcn lacks a YTH domain and a clear match to the R3H domain.
source: However, Bgcn lacks a YTH domain and a clear match to the R3H domain (Figure 10A) and is altered in motifs critical for ATP binding and hydrolysis (Ohlstein et al., 2000) (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by domain analysis in Figure 10A and sequence alignment in Figure 10B, with citation to Ohlstein et al., 2000.

claim: Likely YTHDC2 orthologs were readily found throughout the Eumetazoa subkingdom by BLAST and domain architecture searches.
source: Likely YTHDC2 orthologs were readily found throughout the Eumetazoa subkingdom by BLAST and domain architecture searches (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The complete YTHDC2 domain architecture (R3H, helicase core domains with intact helicase motifs I and II and ARD insertion, HA2, OB, and YTH domains) was the most common form.
source: The complete YTHDC2 domain architecture (R3H, helicase core domains with intact helicase motifs I and II and ARD insertion, HA2, OB, and YTH domains) was the most common form (Figures 8B and 10A,C and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic and domain analysis in Figures 8B, 10A, 10C, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Orthologs of the complete YTHDC2 architecture were present in Cnidaria, the deepest branching eumetazoans examined (Hydra vulgaris and the starlet sea anemone Nematostella vectensis), indicating that full-length YTHDC2 was present in the LCA of the Eumetazoa.
source: Orthologs of this type were present in Cnidaria, the deepest branching eumetazoans examined (Hydra vulgaris and the starlet sea anemone Nematostella vectensis) (Figures 8B and 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2), indicating that full-length YTHDC2 was present in the LCA of the Eumetazoa.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figures 8B, 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homologs with the full domain architecture, except for the YTH domain, were observed in green plants, exemplified by Arabidopsis thaliana NIH (nuclear DEIH-box helicase), and choanoflagellates, e.g., Salpingoeca rosetta.
source: Homologs with the full domain architecture, except for the YTH domain, were observed in green plants, exemplified by Arabidopsis thaliana NIH (nuclear DEIH-box helicase) (Isono et al., 1999), and choanoflagellates, e.g., Salpingoeca rosetta (Genbank accession XP_004993066).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis, with citation to Isono et al., 1999.

claim: The existence of plant homologs suggests an even more ancient evolutionary origin for this protein family.
source: The function of the plant homologs has not been reported to our knowledge, but their existence suggests an even more ancient evolutionary origin for this protein family.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the presence of homologs in plants.

claim: Most metazoan YTHDC2 orthologs are highly conserved; for example, the mouse and H. vulgaris proteins are 44.6% identical.
source: Most metazoan YTHDC2 orthologs are highly conserved; for example, the mouse and H. vulgaris proteins are 44.6% identical.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence comparison.

claim: There were exceptions to YTHDC2 conservation, including apparent sporadic loss of the YTH domain in some species (e.g., platypus and Japanese gekko among vertebrates; and Annelida and Echinodermata among invertebrates).
source: Nonetheless, there were exceptions to this conservation, including apparent sporadic loss of the YTH domain in some species (e.g., platypus and Japanese gekko among vertebrates; and Annelida (e.g., the leech Helobdella robusta) and Echinodermata (the purple sea urchin Strongylocentratus purpuratus) among invertebrates) (Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mode of YTHDC2 binding to RNA can be evolutionarily plastic.
source: Assuming these losses are not errors in genome assembly or annotation, these findings suggest that the mode of YTHDC2 binding to RNA can be evolutionarily plastic.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the observed loss of the YTH domain in some species.

claim: All of the identified YTHDC2 homologs in the phylum Nematoda have a form distinct from other lineages: they retain the R3H, helicase core (including intact helicase motifs I and II), HA2, and OB domains, but they lack a detectable YTH domain.
source: All of the identified YTHDC2 homologs in the phylum Nematoda have a form distinct from other lineages: they retain the R3H, helicase core (including intact helicase motifs I and II), HA2, and OB domains, but they lack a detectable YTH domain.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic and domain analysis (Figures 8B, 10A, 10D, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).

claim: Nematode YTHDC2 homologs have a sequence between the DEXDc and HELICc helicase core domains that aligns poorly with the equivalent region (including the ARD) in other family members, and that is more divergent between nematode species than between most other species.
source: More uniquely, they have a sequence between the DEXDc and HELICc helicase core domains that aligns poorly with the equivalent region (including the ARD) in other family members, and that is more divergent between nematode species than between most other species (Figures 8B and 10A,D, Figure 10—figure supplement 2 and Figure 10—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis in Figures 8B, 10A, 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 2, and Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: Most insect lineages have YTHDC2 orthologs with the full architecture including the YTH domain and intact helicase motifs I and II.
source: Most insect lineages have YTHDC2 orthologs with the full architecture including the YTH domain and intact helicase motifs I and II (Figures 8B and 10C,D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic and domain analysis in Figures 8B, 10C, 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ancestral metazoan form of YTHDC2 was present in the LCA of insects.
source: We conclude that the ancestral metazoan form was present in the LCA of insects.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 10).

claim: Likely orthologs in Hymenoptera (e.g., bees, wasps, ants) and Diptera (e.g., flies, mosquitoes) uniformly lack the YTH domain, suggesting this domain was lost in the LCA of these two clades.
source: However, likely orthologs in Hymenoptera (e.g., bees, wasps, ants) and Diptera (e.g., flies, mosquitoes) uniformly lack the YTH domain, suggesting this domain was lost in the LCA of these two clades.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 10D).

claim: Every species examined in the Schizophora section of flies has a YTHDC2 homolog annotated as an ortholog of D. melanogaster Bgcn.
source: Remarkably, an even more diverged homolog was found specifically in members of the Schizophora section of true flies (Figure 10D). Every species that we examined in this clade has a YTHDC2 homolog annotated as an ortholog of D. melanogaster Bgcn (Figure 10E and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figures 10D and 10E.

claim: Each schizophoran species has a Bgcn-like protein that has the ARD diagnostic of the YTHDC2 family but lacks the YTH domain and has Bgcn-like sequence alterations in helicase motifs I and II that are expected to preclude ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: Each has the ARD diagnostic of the YTHDC2 family but, like Bgcn, lacks the YTH domain and has Bgcn-like sequence alterations in helicase motifs I and II that are expected to preclude ATP binding and hydrolysis (Ohlstein et al., 2000) (Figure 10A,B, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by domain and sequence analysis in Figures 10A, 10B, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2, with citation to Ohlstein et al., 2000.

claim: Most schizophoran flies also have a second YTHDC2 homolog that lacks the YTH domain but that, unlike Bgcn, has intact R3H and helicase motifs I and II.
source: In addition to this protein, most schizophoran flies also have a second YTHDC2 homolog that lacks the YTH domain but that, unlike Bgcn, has intact R3H and helicase motifs I and II (e.g., the house fly Musca domestica and the tephritid fruit flies Rhagoletis zephyria, Ceratitus capetata, and Bactrocera species; Figure 10B,D,E and Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic and sequence analysis in Figures 10B, 10D, 10E, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the Drosophila genomes examined had the more YTHDC2-like version.
source: None of the Drosophila genomes examined had this more YTHDC2-like version (Figure 10D,E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figures 10D and 10E.

claim: The YTH domain was lost before the LCA of Hymenoptera and Diptera, then a gene duplication before the LCA of Schizophora was followed by substantial sequence diversification, creating the Bgcn subfamily.
source: A straightforward interpretation is that the YTH domain was lost before the LCA of Hymenoptera and Diptera, then a gene duplication before the LCA of Schizophora was followed by substantial sequence diversification, creating the Bgcn subfamily.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on phylogenetic analysis (Figure 10).

claim: Most schizophoran species have both YTHDC2-like and Bgcn-like paralogs, but Drosophilidae retain only the Bgcn version.
source: Most schizophoran species have both YTHDC2-like and Bgcn-like paralogs, but Drosophilidae retain only the Bgcn version.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 10).

claim: Although Bgcn is the closest YTHDC2 homolog in D. melanogaster, Bgcn is a paralog of YTHDC2, not its ortholog.
source: Thus, although Bgcn is the closest YTHDC2 homolog in D. melanogaster, Bgcn is a paralog of YTHDC2, not its ortholog.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 10).

claim: A phylogram based on multiple sequence alignments placed one version from each of the non-Drosophila schizophoran species closer to YTHDC2 orthologs from other species, including mouse, and placed the other copy closer to D. melanogaster Bgcn.
source: Supporting this interpretation, a phylogram based on multiple sequence alignments placed one version from each of the non-Drosophila schizophoran species closer to YTHDC2 orthologs from other species, including mouse, and placed the other copy closer to D. melanogaster Bgcn (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 10E.

claim: Bgcn paralogs from Drosophila and non-Drosophila species formed two distinct clusters, and the more YTHDC2-like schizophoran paralogs formed a cluster separated from other YTHDC2 members, including other insect proteins lacking a YTH domain.
source: However, Bgcn paralogs from Drosophila and non-Drosophila species formed two distinct clusters, and the more YTHDC2-like schizophoran paralogs formed a cluster separated from other YTHDC2 members, including other insect proteins lacking a YTH domain (fuchsia branches in Figure 10E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 10E.

claim: Relative to YTHDC2 from non-schizophoran species, there is greater diversity between Bgcn family members within Schizophora and even within Drosophila.
source: Relative to YTHDC2 from non-schizophoran species, there is greater diversity between Bgcn family members within Schizophora and even within Drosophila (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 10E.

claim: Rapid evolution of Bgcn in Drosophila was noted previously, with evidence of positive selection in D. melanogaster and D. simulans but not D. ananassae.
source: Rapid evolution of Bgcn in Drosophila was noted previously, with evidence of positive selection in D. melanogaster and D. simulans (Civetta et al., 2006; Bauer DuMont et al., 2007) but not D. ananassae (Choi and Aquadro, 2014).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Civetta et al., 2006, Bauer DuMont et al., 2007, and Choi and Aquadro, 2014.

claim: MEIOC is highly conserved, with likely orthologs throughout most lineages in Eumetazoa, including Cnidaria.
source: Like YTHDC2, MEIOC is highly conserved, with likely orthologs throughout most lineages in Eumetazoa, including Cnidaria (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017) (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 11A, with citations to Abby et al., 2016 and Soh et al., 2017.

claim: The MEIOC C-terminus contains a domain with a putative coiled-coil motif (DUF4582); this domain is necessary and sufficient for interaction with YTHDC2.
source: The MEIOC C-terminus contains a domain with a putative coiled-coil motif (DUF4582 (domain of unknown function); pfam15189); this domain is necessary and sufficient for interaction with YTHDC2 (Abby et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Abby et al., 2016.

claim: In Eumetazoa, DUF4582 appears to be unique to MEIOC orthologs and is the protein's most highly conserved feature.
source: In Eumetazoa, DUF4582 appears to be unique to MEIOC orthologs and is the protein's most highly conserved feature.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic and domain analysis (Figure 11).

claim: In D. melanogaster, the product of the bag of marbles (bam) gene is a functional collaborator and direct binding partner of Bgcn.
source: In D. melanogaster, the product of the bag of marbles (bam) gene is a functional collaborator and direct binding partner of Bgcn (Gönczy et al., 1997; Lavoie et al., 1999; Ohlstein et al., 2000; Li et al., 2009b; Shen et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010; Insco et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Gönczy et al., 1997, Lavoie et al., 1999, Ohlstein et al., 2000, Li et al., 2009b, Shen et al., 2009, Kim et al., 2010, Insco et al., 2012, and Chen et al., 2014.

claim: By analogy with YTHDC2-MEIOC, it was proposed that Bam may be a functional analog of MEIOC.
source: By analogy with YTHDC2-MEIOC, it was thus proposed that Bam may be a functional analog of MEIOC (Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Soh et al., 2017.

claim: No sequence similarity between MEIOC and Bam has been detected.
source: However, no sequence similarity between MEIOC and Bam has been detected.
evidence: This is stated directly based on the lack of reported sequence similarity.

claim: BLAST searches using mouse or human MEIOC as queries against available dipteran genomes identified no clear homologs, even though homologs containing DUF4582 were easily found in other insect lineages.
source: BLAST searches using mouse or human MEIOC as queries against available dipteran genomes identified no clear homologs (expected (E) value threshold <20), even though homologs containing DUF4582 were easily found in other insect lineages (E < 10−35), including Hymenoptera (e.g., the bumblebee Bombus terrestris) (Figure 11A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 11A.
